title: Starry night at the Atacama Desert coast
caption: The Magellanic Clouds over the Atacama Desert coast, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: From right to left across this sky are the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, two irregular galaxies that neighbor the Milky Way. On the left horizon, a real cloud leans into view.

Magellan's expedition was the first to report these objects, at the beginning of the XVI century. At the time, they were taken for thin clouds that were oddly motionless. Real clouds are common here, because humidity from the cold Pacific Ocean, together with the temperature contrast with the ground, often blankets the Atacama Desert's shoreline. That moisture feeds the local plants, many kinds of cacti, a lot of them found nowhere else.

The cold ocean also keeps the so-called inversion layer very low, leaving the air above the clouds exceptionally dry and clear. Those are the conditions at Paranal Observatory, 2600 meters up and only 12 km from the coast. It is home to ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), which ESO calls the most advanced optical ground-based telescope in the world.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by G. Hüdepohl. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Magellanic Clouds may look brighter and more defined here than to someone on the coast.
